explanation:
## About 119.2 MiB

```
10^9 bits / 8            = 125,000,000 bytes
125,000,000 / 1,048,576  = 119.2 MiB
```

Note the distinction the question leans on: it is **125 MB** in decimal units and **119.2 MiB** in binary ones. Disk manufacturers quote the first; `free`, `top` and every programmer quote the second. A 5% discrepancy is small enough to look like a rounding error and large enough to matter in a capacity estimate.

## What the alternatives cost

| Representation | Per candidate | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `std::bitset` / packed bits | 1 bit | **119 MiB** |
| `std::vector<bool>` | 1 bit (it is specialised) | 119 MiB |
| `bool[]` or `char[]` | 1 byte | 954 MiB |
| `int[]` | 4 bytes | 3.7 GiB |

The naive `bool[]` is eight times larger, and `int[]` thirty-two times. On a laptop with 8 GiB, the `int[]` version does not run and the `bool[]` version swaps.

## The memory saving is not really the point

The eight-times reduction matters far less than what it does to the **cache**.

A sieve's inner loop marks multiples of `p`, striding by `p`. With one byte per candidate, consecutive marks for `p = 3` are 3 bytes apart — about 21 marks per 64-byte line. With one bit, they are 3 *bits* apart, so one line covers 512 candidates and roughly 170 marks. Many times fewer lines fetched for the same work.

More importantly, the whole working set shrinks by eight. A segment of the sieve that did not fit in a 32 MiB L3 now does, and the difference between an L3 hit and a DRAM reference is about fifty times. This is the recurring theme of the subject: **a representation change that reduces memory is usually a performance change, and usually a bigger one than you expected.**

## Two standard further reductions

**Skip the evens.** Every even number above 2 is composite, so store only odd candidates: 5*10^8 bits, **59.6 MiB**. Index `i` means the number `2i+1`. Halves memory, halves the traffic, costs one line of index arithmetic.

**Wheel factorisation.** Skip multiples of 2, 3 and 5 as well, storing only the 8 residues coprime to 30 out of every 30 integers. That is `8/30` of the candidates, about **31.8 MiB** — a 3.75x reduction over the plain bitset. The indexing gets fiddly and this is where most high-performance sieves stop.

## Segmenting is the real answer at scale

Even 119 MiB does not fit in cache, so a monolithic sieve to 10^9 is bound by DRAM bandwidth. A **segmented sieve** processes a window of, say, 256 KiB at a time — sized to fit L2 — crossing off multiples of the primes below `sqrt(10^9)` which is about 31,623, and those primes themselves need only a tiny 4 KiB sieve.

Each segment is swept entirely within cache, so the main array is touched once sequentially rather than repeatedly at a stride. The arithmetic is identical; the memory behaviour is not, and the speedup is typically several times. It is the same move as tiling a matrix transpose, applied to a completely different algorithm — which is the reason both are worth knowing as one idea rather than two.

## `vector<bool>` deserves its reputation

`std::vector<bool>` is specialised to pack bits, which is exactly what you want here — and it is also why it is not a real container: `operator[]` returns a proxy object rather than a reference, so `auto& b = v[0]` does not compile and `&v[0]` is meaningless. For a sieve that is fine and it is a reasonable choice. For anything generic, `std::bitset` (fixed size) or a hand-rolled `vector<uint64_t>` is clearer about what it is doing.
